opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this actually started as kind of a fun side thing. I'd sit down and ask these models, "Tell me a new joke," and what I kept getting back was, almost invariably, a joke I'd heard before. You know, the "why don't scientists trust atoms? Because they make up everything" kind of thing. And even when you push it and say, "No, something original, something nobody's heard," it would often just do a light remix of a known joke, swap a noun or two, and the punchline would kind of fall apart.

What struck me was that jokes are such a nice test case, because the structure is very familiar. There's a setup, there's a twist, there's a punchline that recontextualizes the setup. The models clearly know that template extremely well. But the hard part of a joke isn't the template, it's finding that surprising connection that still feels inevitable once you hear it. And that's exactly where they struggled.

So it shaped my thinking in a few ways. One, it made me much more skeptical of evaluations where we see fluent, well-structured output and conclude the model is being creative. Fluency within a structure is not the same as novelty. Two, it suggested that the way we train these models, especially next-token prediction followed by things like RLHF, pushes them toward the high-likelihood, safe region of the distribution. And a good joke, almost by definition, lives somewhere lower-probability but still coherent. There's a tension there.

And three, it got me interested in whether this is fundamental or whether it's a training artifact. Could you design objectives or decoding strategies, or even think about planning-style approaches where the model works backward from a punchline, that actually let it explore more? That's become a real research question for us, not just in jokes but in things like generating novel problems or research ideas, where you want something genuinely new but still grounded in a structure people recognize.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated prompts for new, original jokes produced familiar jokes or weak remixes, and explains that the models knew the joke template but struggled to create a surprising connection within it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was actually kind of a fun little exercise that ended up being more informative than I expected. I was playing around, asking models to write me a new joke, and the thing that struck me is that they're very, very good at the form. You get the setup, you get the beat, you get something that has the rhythm of a punchline. Structurally, it's unmistakably a joke. But then you read it and it's just... not funny. Or it's funny because you've heard it before. A lot of the time, if you dig a little, the "new" joke is a pretty light remix of something that's very common on the internet.

And I think that captures something important about how I think about novelty with these models. There's a difference between generating something that's novel in the sense of being a new string that hasn't appeared verbatim before, and novel in the sense of actually introducing a new idea into a familiar structure. The models are extremely good at the first thing and I'd say surprisingly weak at the second. Jokes are a nice test case because the structure is so rigid and so well-represented in the training data that the model can fully nail the template, and so the failure is isolated. You can see exactly where the gap is. The gap is in the part that requires the actual creative leap, the unexpected connection between two things that haven't been connected before.

What's interesting from a research perspective is that this lines up with what we see in more controlled settings. If you look at the distribution of outputs, there's a strong pull toward the mode. The model wants to produce the high-probability thing, and a good joke is by definition a low-probability thing that nonetheless makes sense. So there's a tension built into how these models are trained and how we decode from them. You can try to push against it with temperature or with clever prompting, but often what you get is either more of the same or incoherence, not the sweet spot in between.

So I came away thinking that "can it produce something new within a familiar structure" is actually a really good lens for creativity more broadly, and that jokes are a surprisingly honest benchmark for that. Honest because you can't fake it. Either it lands or it doesn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models reliably produce joke structure but struggle to introduce a genuinely new idea, often remixing familiar jokes.

astra-6.text:
I think jokes are an interesting test because there’s a familiar structure, but the surprise is really the point. When I tried prompting language models for new jokes, my impression was that they were much better at producing something that looked like a joke than at making it feel genuinely fresh. You could change the subject or the wording, but that didn’t necessarily give you a new idea.

That made me distinguish between following a structure and doing something interesting within it. A model can capture the pattern very well, and that’s impressive, but it doesn’t by itself tell us how well it can generate a new twist. And, of course, whether I find a joke surprising is a subjective test—it’s not a definitive measure of what the model can create.

r001.rationale: The response says the models could produce something that looked like a joke but struggled to make it feel genuinely fresh, even when the subject or wording changed.

sol-6.1.text:
When I tried prompting language models for new jokes, what struck me was how hard it was to judge whether they were actually producing something new. A joke could be unfamiliar to me, but that doesn’t mean the model invented it. And changing a few details in a familiar joke isn’t necessarily the kind of novelty we have in mind either.

But there’s an interesting distinction there: you can work within a familiar structure and still produce something new. The structure of a joke gives you constraints, but the surprise has to come from somewhere. So I came away thinking that simply asking for a “new joke” isn’t a very clean test of creativity. You need to be more precise about what’s new—the wording, the combination of ideas, or the underlying insight.

r001.rationale: The response says it was hard to judge whether a joke was genuinely new; it does not say the models struggled to generate new jokes within a familiar structure.
